primary_source.title: An Investigation of the Therac-25 Accidents
primary_source.publication: IEEE Computer, Vol. 26, No. 7, July 1993, pp. 18-41
primary_source.why_authoritative: Definitive academic investigation by the foremost software safety researchers

timeline_events.event: Therac-25 introduced. Hardware interlocks removed, software handles all safety
AECL safety analysis apparently excludes software analysis
Katherine Yarbrough (61) overdosed at Kennestone, Marietta GA. 15,000-20,000 rad vs 200 rad prescribed
Frances Hill (40) overdosed at Ontario Cancer Foundation, Hamilton ON. 13,000-17,000 rad
Frances Hill dies from cancer. Autopsy notes radiation damage
Woman overdosed at Yakima Valley Memorial Hospital, WA
AECL claims Therac-25 could not have been responsible for Yakima injuries
Voyne Ray Cox overdosed at East Texas Cancer Center, Tyler TX. 16,500-25,000 rad in <1 second
Verdon Kidd overdosed at ETCC Tyler during facial treatment. Fritz Hager discovers overdose extent
Verdon Kidd dies - first official death from therapeutic radiation accident
FDA declares Therac-25 defective, demands Corrective Action Plan
Voyne Ray Cox dies from radiation burns
Glen A. Dodd (65) overdosed at Yakima. 8,000-10,000 rad vs 86 rad prescribed
FDA issues Notice of Adverse Findings. Recommends all units removed from service
Glen A. Dodd dies from radiation complications
AECL sends fifth and final CAP revision to FDA
AECL dissolves Medical section. Theratronics assumes maintenance

data_points.claim: Therac-25 removed hardware safety interlocks present in Therac-6 and Therac-20
At least three patients died (Kidd May 1986, Cox Aug 1986, Dodd Apr 1987)
Yarbrough received 15,000-20,000 rad vs prescribed 200 rad (75-100x overdose)
Race condition: mode change within 8-second window caused beam to fire without target
Arithmetic overflow: Class3 variable (1 byte, max 255) rolled to 0, bypassing safety check
Malfunction 54 was undocumented; operators pressed P to proceed past it
Software written in PDP-11 assembly by single programmer over several years
Full CAP took more than two years after first Tyler accident
Ray Cox received 16,500-25,000 rad in <1 second over 1 cm2
FDA: 'impossible for CDRH to find all potential failure modes of the software'
Final CAP Revision 5 included 23+ changes including reinstated hardware interlocks

Per-accident display behavior: in the FIRST accident (Kennestone, Marietta GA, June 1985) the machine gave NO overdose indication - its readouts indicated a normal treatment, which is why physicist Tim Still had to inquire and AECL could assert an overdose was impossible. The undocumented MALFUNCTION 54 error code belongs to the LATER Tyler, Texas accidents (March/April 1986). Fact-vetting note: do not flag narration of the first accident (no alarm / treatment read as normal) as contradicting the Malfunction 54 data point - they are different accidents.

unverifiable_claims: Patient names (Yarbrough, Hill, Cox, Kidd, Dodd) appear in secondary sources but NOT in the Leveson/Turner primary paper
Exact dose figures vary between sources (e.g., 100x vs 75-100x for Yarbrough)
Some secondary sources describe Kidd as 'first person to die from a software bug' which is an editorial characterization

misconceptions: One bug caused all accidents (there were at least two distinct bugs)
The programmer was negligent (software reused from models with hardware backups)
FDA failed to act (declared defective May 1986 but lacked technical resources)
